newsitem.title: UK: U.S. rate-watch on agenda for emerging markets.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rate-watch on agenda for emerging markets.

text.p: Emerging market investors will be watching U.S. data this week for signs that interest rates might rise, while politics in Russia and Brazil and unrest in South Korea and Bulgaria will increase uncertainty, strategists say.

U.S. Treasury markets stabilised on Monday after long bond yields soared on Friday but with U.S. retail sales and consumer price data due on Tuesday, investors are seeking clues on whether interest rates there might rise.

"I think it is premature to say this means the Fed (Federal Reserve) will tighten soon but it brings forward the possibility and makes it more certain that the next move is upwards," said Richard Gray, emerging market analyst at BankAmerica, after Friday's stronger than expected December U.S. jobs data.
The strong U.S. figures included a surprising 262,000 increase in non-farm payrolls for December, far exceeding forecasts and raising the spectre of higher interest rates.
Latin America's stock markets, with their close ties to the U.S. economy, will feel the pain from a U.S. rate rise mainly if it impacts on Wall Street.
But Argentine debt, and to a lesser extent Mexico's, is more vulnerable since the Argentine peso is pegged to the dollar.
ARGENTINA begins roadshows for a $2 billion dual tranche global bond this week and Gray said Friday's U.S. data might make its launch more difficult.
"It is now a more awkward market," he said. "They are not going to have a lot of comfort until the Fed tightens."
The earliest this could happen is at the February 4 meeting of the U.S. Federal Reserve, though Gray thought the Fed might hold off until March.
The growing consensus over the direction of U.S. interest rates coincides with events in individual developing countries like RUSSIA and BRAZIL, both facing key weeks for their leaders.

"I'm still concerned about the health of President (Boris) Yeltsin," said Ousmene Mandeng, emerging market strategist at WestMerchant, after the Russian president unnerved debt markets last week when he was taken to hospital with pneumonia.
The news failed to dent equity markets, which soared to highs on strong trading volume.
The International Monetary Fund returns to Moscow on Monday for talks on the economy which investors hope will lead to the release of a delayed loan tranche.
Meanwhile, the re-election dreams of BRAZIL's President Fernando Henrique Cardoso face their first hurdle this week in the form of a legislative committee vote.
Foreign investors are starting to anticipate the likelihood of the necessary constitutional amendment being passed.
"The re-election bill in Brazil is increasingly likely to be passed by Congress, possibly as early as (this) week," ANZ Grindlays said in a note to investors.

Others, however, are waiting for Brazil's December import figures this week to complete the month's trade balance picture after the release last week of export data that analysts said looked reasonable.

The situation in BULGARIA, meanwhile, is unlikely to bring much joy to investors in the near term, with trade unions planning a wave of strikes to pressure the ruling Socialists into holding an early general election.
Investors had been hoping Bulgarian politics would stabilise over the weekend so the country could turn to steadying the ailing economy via the implementation of IMF reforms.
But prospects for this now look bleak as protests sparked by severe economic hardship escalate into industrial strife.
The situation was complicated on Friday when President Zhelyu Zhelev postponed giving a mandate to the Socialist prime minister-designate, Nikolai Dobrev, to form a new government.
While PERU's markets have held up reasonably well during the hostage crisis, pressure is still on President Alberto Fujimori.

"So far debt prices have come down but not tremendously and that is a sign people do believe the crisis will be solved and that Peru's situation will not be undermined significantly," said one strategist. "But if there is bloodshed, then it may be that that perception has to be revised."
Others say fear the incident could threaten Peru's economy.
"This terrorist incident is likely to shake investor and consumer confidence and could potentially threaten the expected recovery," Foreign & Colonial strategists said.
How the SOUTH KOREAN government handles a wave of strikes that began December 26 will preoccupy investors in Asian equities.
But F&C for one said it did not believe the government would have to backtrack on the new labour law that sparked the strife.
"The new law is in fact positive for the long term and we do not believe that the government will be forced to negotiate on the issue," it said.
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, IFC/IPRD, denominated in dollars, was up 3.9 percent at 305.93 points on Friday, compared with a week ago.
Latin America was up 6.0 percent week-on-week at 567.54, Asia was up 2.4 percent at 258.48 and Europe, Middle East and Africa as a region was up 4.1 at 139.75.
